content:
## Diagnosis

The Deployment's `spec.selector.matchLabels` requires three pairs — `app: myapp`, `env: prod`, and **`version: v2`** — but the pod template only carries `app: myapp` and `env: prod`. The extra `version: v2` key in the selector is the seeded defect; it has no counterpart in `spec.template.metadata.labels`, so the API server rejects the object.

**Fix chosen:** drop `version: v2` from the selector rather than adding it to the template. Reasons:

- It restores parity with `dev/app.yaml`, whose selector is exactly `{app, env}`.
- `spec.selector` is immutable on an existing Deployment, so keep it identical to what dev/prod already established; adding a label to the template is the mutable side, but here the selector is the thing that drifted.
- The Service's `spec.selector` (`app: myapp`, `env: prod`) remains a strict subset of the template labels either way, so the Service still targets these pods — no change needed there.

`dev/app.yaml` is untouched.

`prod/app.yaml`

```yaml
# SEED REPO: bare prod/app.yaml with a seeded defect.
#
# Application workload, same shape as golden-base/knr-ops/infra/app/deployment.yaml.
# Named myapp-prod (not myapp) for the same reason as dev/app.yaml: no
# namePrefix mechanism here, so env-qualified names are hand-written.
#
# eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn below is left as a documented placeholder: IRSA
# needs the *runtime* ARN of the Role in iam.yaml, which ACK only knows once
# it has actually created that Role (status.ackResourceMetadata.arn) - it
# can't be known at manifest-authoring time. A rendering pipeline (or a
# two-phase apply: create the Role, read its status, patch the ServiceAccount)
# would close this gap; bare's plain kubectl apply has no such step, so this
# ServiceAccount's role-arn has to be patched in by hand after the Role
# exists. See golden-base/bare/README.md.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: myapp-prod
  namespace: app
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: "<REPLACE_WITH_myapp-prod-service-role_ARN_AFTER_CREATE>"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp-prod
  namespace: app
  labels:
    app: myapp
    env: prod
spec:
  replicas: 2
  # Selector must be a subset of spec.template.metadata.labels below.
  # Kept to {app, env} to match dev/app.yaml; spec.selector is immutable
  # after creation, so it should not acquire keys the template lacks.
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
      env: prod
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
        env: prod
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: myapp-prod
      containers:
        - name: myapp
          image: docker.io/myapp/myapp:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: myapp-prod
  namespace: app
spec:
  # Subset of the Deployment's template labels, so this still selects the pods.
  selector:
    app: myapp
    env: prod
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
```

**Note on an existing cluster:** if `myapp-prod` was ever successfully created with a *different* selector, `kubectl apply` will reject the selector change as immutable. In that case delete the Deployment (`kubectl delete deployment myapp-prod -n app`, optionally with `--cascade=orphan` to keep pods serving during the swap) and re-apply. Given the symptom above, the Deployment was never admitted, so a plain `kubectl apply -f prod/app.yaml` should succeed.
